items.title: What the list row carries and what it leaves out
items.body:
The key is right. `TicketSummaryDto` has id, number, subject, customer name and email, status, priority, assignment, tags, timestamps, two breach flags, `CommentCount` and `Version`. It has no `Description` and no comment list; those are in `TicketDetailDto`, where comments are filtered by `CanReadInternalNotes`.

- Customer name and email are in the summary.
- `Version` is in both records.
- Tags and both breach flags are summary fields.

excerpts.quote: int CommentCount, int Version);
it deliberately has no description or comment bodies.

items.title: An undefined enum falls through to the default arm
items.body:
The key is right. A C# enum is an integer underneath, so a JSON body can carry `(TicketPriority)99`. Before the fix, `Ticket.Create` had no `Enum.IsDefined` check. Neither SLA switch had an arm for 99, so both used `_ =>`: `now.AddBusinessHours(8)` and `now.AddDays(5)`, the Low due dates.

- Casting an int to an enum never throws in C#.
- Urgent is a named arm; 99 does not match it.
- Both switches return a value for every input, thanks to `_ =>`.

excerpts.quote: the two SLA `switch` expressions fell through to their `_ =>` arm, so the ticket got the *Low* due dates while reporting priority 99.
_ => now.AddBusinessHours(8)

items.title: Filter by permission, then page
items.body:
The key is right. If the handler paged first, a customer whose only ticket sits on the second source page would get an empty page one and a wrong total. The guide states it directly, and the 121-ticket test proves it.

- Speed is not the reason; the guide warns that this in-memory loop would be a table scan at scale.
- The store applies only text and field filters; it knows nothing about the user.
- `Skip`/`Take` work on any list; they never throw because of who can read a row.

excerpts.quote: If page one contains 100 records the customer cannot read, a matching record on source page two would disappear from the final page and the total would describe the wrong population.
var items = visible.Skip((page - 1) * pageSize).Take(pageSize).ToList();

items.title: Core idea: rows the store returns versus rows you may read
items.body:
Search mixes two questions. The store answers "which tickets match these filters?". The permission policy answers "which of those may this user see?". Paging (page number and page size) must be applied to the answer of the second question, or the page and the total count describe the wrong set of rows.

While reading `SearchTickets.cs`, notice there are two kinds of page: the source pages the handler pulls from the store, and the page the user asked for. Then compare the in-memory loop with the EF Core sketch in chapter 02, where the same rule becomes one query with a WHERE clause.

excerpts.quote: Search has two populations: records returned by the store and records the current user may read.
build one `IQueryable`, apply the ownership predicate **first**, count and page **on the same query**, and only then materialise.

readMore.why: The 35-line handler: find the source-page loop and the final Skip/Take.

items.title: Trim, lowercase, dedupe, sort, then one version bump
items.body:
The key is right. `NormalizeTag` trims and lowercases, so the input becomes billing, billing, vip. `Distinct` (case-insensitive) keeps one billing. `Order()` sorts, and "billing" sorts before "vip". `Touch` runs once at the end of the method, so Version goes up by one.

- The casing is not kept: `ToLowerInvariant` runs on every tag.
- Duplicates are removed by `Distinct`.
- Version changes once per call, not once per tag, and the order is alphabetical.

excerpts.quote: private static string NormalizeTag(string tag) => tag.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
`NormalizeTag` trims and lowercases; `Distinct` ignores case; `Order` stabilizes the result.

items.title: An internal note needs a staff role
items.body:
The key is right. `CanComment` switches on the requested visibility. The `Internal` arm is `(user.Role is SupportRole.Admin or SupportRole.Manager or SupportRole.Agent) && CanReadTicket(user, ticket)`. A customer fails the role test, so the result is false whatever their email.

- The email clause appears only in the `_` (public) arm.
- The handler does not rewrite visibility; it asks the policy and refuses.
- Customers can comment publicly on their own ticket; only the internal kind is refused.

excerpts.quote: CommentVisibility.Internal => (user.Role is SupportRole.Admin or SupportRole.Manager or SupportRole.Agent) && CanReadTicket(user, ticket),
`CanComment` receives the requested visibility, so a customer cannot switch a public reply to an internal note by changing one JSON enum.

items.title: The second writer is rejected before it mutates
items.body:
The key is right. Both requests enter `UpdateAsync`, and `lock (_writeLock)` lets one in at a time. The first moves the ticket to version 4. The second compares `current.Version` (4) with its `expectedVersion` (3) and throws `ConcurrencyException`. The throw comes before `current.Snapshot()` and `mutate(workingCopy)`, so its change never runs.

- The lock serializes the writes; it does not let a stale one through.
- The store never retries; there is no retry or merge logic in `UpdateAsync`.
- Nothing waits for an old version; the check fails at once.

excerpts.quote: if (current.Version != expectedVersion)
The second reads current version 4, fails the equality check, and throws `ConcurrencyException`; its working copy is never mutated

items.title: One connection per mount, state through refs
items.body:
The key is right. The effect's cleanup calls `connection.stop()`. With `[selectedId, filters]` as dependencies, every change re-ran the effect: stop the socket, open a new one, rejoin the group. The fix keeps `[]` and reads the changing values from `filtersRef.current` and `selectedIdRef.current`.

- SignalR has no one-handler limit that forced this.
- A ref never causes a re-render; the guide says refs are not reactive.
- With `[]` and no ref, the callback would see only mount-time values, the opposite failure.

excerpts.quote: Adding `filters` or `selectedId` here would
So every keystroke in the search box tore down a WebSocket and opened a new one, re-ran `JoinInbox`, and left a window in which a `tickets.changed` event reached nobody.

items.title: Start here: follow one support ticket through the stack
items.body:
SupportDesk (in `support-ticketing-app/`) is a help-desk demo: an ASP.NET Core API with an in-memory store, SignalR for live updates, and a React inbox. The course in `astraupskill/` follows one ticket from the browser to the domain object and back.

Suggested order:

1. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: which file owns which decision.
2. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: who may see a ticket, and why that check happens before paging.
3. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`: safe mutation, version numbers, and the data-free SignalR event.
4. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`: the four xUnit facts and what they prove.
5. `07-TRACE-LAB.md`: step-by-step traces, plus the React ref lesson.

Keep `Ticket.cs`, `InMemoryTicketStore.cs`, `Permissions.cs` and `SearchTickets.cs` open while reading; most quiz questions point at a few lines in them.

excerpts.quote: This nine-file course follows a support ticket through domain mutation, optimistic concurrency, permission-aware search, a data-free SignalR invalidation, and the React refresh that follows it.

readMore.why: The whole role policy fits on one screen; read every rule once.
The exact test file, reproduced in the guide.

items.title: ToArray is the safety line in ReplaceTags
items.body:
The key is right. LINQ is lazy: nothing in `tags.Select(...).Where(...).Distinct(...).Order()` runs until `.ToArray()` pulls the items. If the input throws while being read, the exception happens at `ToArray`, before `_tags.Clear()` and before `Touch`. So the old tags and the old Version stay.

- `_tags.Clear()` is the next statement after `ToArray`, so it has not run.
- "changed" was only inside the half-built pipeline; it never reached `_tags`.
- `Touch` is the last line, so Version cannot have moved.

excerpts.quote: .Where(tag => tag.Length > 0).Distinct(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase).Order().ToArray();
If an enumerable yields `changed` and then throws, `_tags.Clear()` has not run, so the original tags and version remain intact.

items.title: Core idea: optimistic versions and an event that carries nothing
items.body:
Every ticket has a `Version` number. A client sends the version it last read with each change, and the store refuses the write if the ticket has moved on since. This is optimistic concurrency: no one holds a lock while editing; a stale editor is told to refresh.

After a successful change, the server tells browsers that something changed, but does not say what. Each browser then asks again over normal HTTP, where the permission checks run. Read `UpdateAsync` in the store, `Touch` in `Ticket.cs`, and the notifier class, and ask: what could a broadcast leak if it did carry data?

excerpts.quote: A successful domain method calls `Touch(now)`, updates `UpdatedAt`, and increments `Version` exactly once.
This is optimistic concurrency for one in-memory process.

readMore.why: UpdateAsync, the lock and the version comparison.

items.title: Counting the store calls
items.body:
The key is right. Each call asks the store for `PageSize = 100` (the caller's 50 is not used here). The loop condition is `sourcePage <= Math.Max(1, (int)Math.Ceiling(searchResult.Total / 100d))`; with 121 rows that is 2, so the handler calls the store twice and only then applies the caller's page of 50.

- One call at size 50 would be paging before filtering, the old bug.
- Three calls of 50 is not what the code requests: the source page size is fixed at 100.
- The loop has no early exit when it finds a visible row; it reads every source page.

excerpts.quote: searchResult = await _store.SearchAsync(criteria with { Page = sourcePage, PageSize = 100 }, cancellationToken);
} while (sourcePage <= Math.Max(1, (int)Math.Ceiling(searchResult.Total / 100d)));

items.title: Internal notes never take part in search
items.body:
The key is right: the comment clause in `InMemoryTicketStore.SearchAsync` is `comment.Visibility == CommentVisibility.Public && comment.Body.Contains(term, ...)`. An internal note cannot match, so the customer gets zero items and a total of 0, as the test asserts.

- Customers cannot read internal comments: `CanReadInternalNotes` is staff-only.
- The ticket is not returned at all, because the match fails before any DTO is built.
- No 403 is involved; it is an ordinary empty result.

excerpts.quote: ticket.Comments.Any(comment => comment.Visibility == CommentVisibility.Public && comment.Body.Contains(term, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)));
An internal comment body cannot make a customer's search return a ticket, even if the customer happens to know the marker.

items.title: The SignalR event is only a doorbell
items.body:
The key is right: `TicketUpdatedAsync` is `_hub.Clients.Group("inbox").SendAsync("tickets.changed", cancellationToken)`. No argument after the method name, so no ticket data travels. The `ticket` parameter only satisfies the interface.

- Sending the summary DTO to the whole inbox group would leak customer email to every connection.
- No id or version is sent; clients refetch the list and the selected detail.
- The hub does no per-connection filtering; the HTTP detail endpoint does that later.

excerpts.quote: _hub.Clients.Group("inbox").SendAsync("tickets.changed", cancellationToken);
The argument `ticket` is used only to satisfy the application interface; it is not serialized.

items.title: Why the customer ticket lands on the second source page
items.body:
The key is right. The store orders by `UpdatedAt` descending. The test creates T-000001 at `now` and the other 120 tickets at `now.AddSeconds(i)`, so all of them are newer. T-000001 is therefore row 121, which is on source page 2 when pages hold 100.

- The store never sorts by `Number`, and source pages hold 100 rows.
- Insertion order into a `ConcurrentDictionary` does not decide the result order; the explicit sort does.
- Comments do not affect the sort key.

excerpts.quote: var ordered = query.OrderByDescending(ticket => ticket.UpdatedAt).ToList();
`T-000001` is row 121 — on source page 2.
